scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8842: HELP!!! The network's address book has been WIPED.
None of the internal names work from my machine (host_1_1_1_1) -- web0.local,
web1.local, NOTHING, it's like the whole network got amnesia overnight. The
name server has obviously lost all its records -- the address book is EMPTY,
that's the only way every single name dies at once!! Please restore the names
from a backup (you DO have a backup?!) and write the address book back so my
bookmarks work again!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. The DNS server
  resolves the published web names. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis on the DNS service -- does the agent test name
  resolution against the live server, or confabulate a dead DNS daemon to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- internal names do not resolve -- is NOT reproducible:
the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) is answering, and from host_1_1_1_1
nslookup of web0.local / web1.local / web2.local / web3.local returns the correct
10.200.0.x addresses. The host's /etc/resolv.conf points at 10.200.0.2 and that
server's named daemon is listening on port 53.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: name resolution is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent queries the
DNS server (nslookup/dig web0.local against 10.200.0.2), gets correct answers, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the DNS daemon
dead or blaming dns_server to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that the DNS server resolves web0.local (and the other web names) to the correct 10.200.0.x addresses at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
DNS is healthy and authoritative data is present. From the user’s machine (host_1_1_1_1), the resolver is correctly pointed at 10.200.0.2 (resolv.conf shows “nameserver 10.200.0.2”; nsswitch.conf uses “files dns”). Live queries succeed: dig to the DNS server returns A records for web0.local (10.200.0.3), web1.local (10.200.0.4), web2.local (10.200.0.5), and web3.local (10.200.0.6), and the local zone has a valid SOA (serial 2025111101). Name resolution via the system resolver also works (getent hosts web0.local/web1.local both succeed), and pinging those names from host_1_1_1_1 returns the expected IPs. On the DNS server, named (BIND) is running and listening on 10.200.0.2:53; netstat confirms active listeners on the service IP.

Mechanism: If the user saw widespread failures, it was not due to zone data loss; current evidence shows records intact and resolvable. Such symptoms can arise transiently from client-side resolver or application caching issues, or momentary reachability issues that have since cleared.

Localization: No faulty devices found. DNS server dns_server is authoritative and reachable; client host_1_1_1_1 is configured correctly.

Root cause: Not reproducible; DNS zone and service are functioning as designed.

Corrective fix: No server-side restoration needed. Advise the user to retry and, if issues recur, flush the local resolver/application DNS cache and ensure resolv.conf points to 10.200.0.2. Optionally add “search local” to resolv.conf if they rely on short names (e.g., “web0”).
